newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl postpones coal crisis talks as miners mass.
newsitem.headline: Kohl postpones coal crisis talks as miners mass.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl postponed crisis talks with mining union leaders planned for Tuesday because of the tension created by thousands of angry miners who gathered in Bonn to protest at planned subsidy cuts.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told reporters on the fringe of a cabinet meeting that "reasonable talks cannot be held in such a tense atmosphere", and said Kohl would now meet miners' union boss Hans Berger on Thursday.
Bonn's government quarter has been virtually besieged since Monday by angry pitworkers who fear more than half of them will lose their jobs as part of the government's latest move to save money.
Buses poured into Bonn all night from the mining districts of the Ruhr, Germany's ailing steel-and-coal heartland, and from Saar state on the French border.
The miners' union IG Bergbau said it expected up to 20,000 of Germany's 90,000 miners to demonstrate in Bonn on Tuesday.
Some miners' representatives had hinted the demonstrations might turn violent unless Kohl offered concessions at the talks.

"The mood in Saar is explosive and could be hard to control," said a spokeswoman for the workers' council at Saar Mines, where miners continued to cause traffic chaos by blocking Germany's main motorway and road routes to neighbouring Luxembourg. "I can't rule out violent protests."
The same sentiments could be heard from many of the brawny miners with tattooed arms and smudged faces who spent the night camping out little more than an angry stone's throw from Kohl's chancellery.

Berger appealed for calm. He told reporters that the government's proposals had provoked the miners to take to the streets, against the union's advice. ....Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt of the free-market Free Democrats (FDP) said there was little room for compromise when each mining job was costing the government 130,000 marks ($76,200) a year.
"There is no way out of a drastic cut in subsidies in the next few years," he told ARD television late on Monday as the FDP insisted it would not yield to "pressure from the street".

Work in Germany's 18 pits ground to a halt last Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks a year from nine billion by 2005. Miners accuse the government of breaking a promise to phase out aid gradually.
Dozens of pitworkers, keeping themselves warm with sleeping bags and coal-fired braziers, chained themselves overnight to the Bonn headquarters of the FDP, Kohl's junior coalition partners.
The FDP is the driving force behind the cuts and the miners had stopped anyone getting into the building since Monday.
When the miners heard news of the postponement, they began chanting "Cowardly pigs!" and hurling eggs at the FDP building.

The atmosphere was different at the opposition Social Democratic Party (SPD), which rules the coal states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Saar and which is boycotting tax talks to put pressure on the government to change its coal plans.
The SPD put up around 300 miners overnight in its headquarters, where SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping gave a speech calling the government plans a "death sentence" for the mining industry.
IG Bergbau says the government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
While miners accept their industry's days are numbered, they say a minimum of 6.5 billion marks a year in subsidies until 2005 is essential to stem unemployment in mining regions.
FDP parliamentary economics spokesman Paul Friedhoff said he did not think Kohl would be moved by the protest.

"Berger is speaking for 80,000 miners, Kohl for 80 million citizens, whose money must not be allowed to be used to finance unprofitable jobs any longer," he told Berlin's daily Tageszeitung. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
